hints: Look at the parent group on the ring, the $\text{COOH}$ group makes the parent benzoic acid, then number the second substituent relative to carbon 1.
walkthrough:
Spot the parent acid**
When $\text{COOH}$ is directly attached to a benzene ring, the parent name is benzoic acid. That carbon with the $\text{COOH}$ is always carbon 1, you do not need to number it.

Number the nitro group**
In P the $\text{NO}_2$ group is on the carbon right next to the $\text{COOH}$, that is the ortho position which is position 2. Put them together to get 2-nitrobenzoic acid.

hints: Compare the two structures in Fig. 7.2 and focus on what changes, a $\text{CH}_3$ group attached to the ring becomes a $\text{COOH}$ group while the $\text{NO}_2$ group is unchanged.
walkthrough:
Recognise a side chain oxidation**
You are converting $\text{Ar-CH}_3$ to $\text{Ar-COOH}$. The ring and the $\text{NO}_2$ group stay exactly the same. This is the classic vigorous oxidation of an alkyl side chain to a carboxylic acid.

Recall the strong oxidiser**
The reagent for this is potassium manganate(VII), $\text{KMnO}_4$, heated under reflux. It can be used in alkaline, acidic or neutral conditions, with heating essential to force the $\text{CH}_3$ all the way up to $\text{COOH}$.
Final answer: Heat / reflux with alkaline or acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ / $\text{MnO}_4^-$ (followed by acidification if alkaline).

hints: Think about the directing behaviour of the group already on the ring, the $\text{COOH}$ group, in nitration by electrophilic substitution.
walkthrough:
Link the existing group to where the new group goes**
In electrophilic substitution, the group already on the ring controls the position of attack. $\text{COOH}$ pulls electrons away from the ring by its electron withdrawing effect.

Apply meta direction**
Electron withdrawing groups like $\text{COOH}$ destabilise the intermediate for ortho and para attack, so they direct the incoming $\text{NO}_2^+$ electrophile to the meta positions, carbons 3 and 5. That is why the meta isomer T dominates and the ortho isomer P is only a minor product.

Final answer: $\text{COOH}$ is an electron-withdrawing deactivating group and is meta-directing, so nitration occurs mainly at the 3- and 5-positions to give T rather than the 2- (ortho) position of P.

hints: Work backwards from methyl red, the left ring with $\text{COOH}$ must come from P, so step 1 must change $\text{NO}_2$ into a group that can later form the $\text{N=N}$ link.
Recall the standard two step sequence to make an azo dye, $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$ then $\text{NH}_2$ to diazonium $\text{N}_2^+$ for coupling.
Look at the right hand ring of methyl red, it contains $\text{N(CH}_3)_2$ para to the azo link, so S must supply that activated ring for coupling in step 3.
walkthrough:
Decode Q from step 1**
P has $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ ortho to each other. Step 1 followed by diazotisation in step 2 tells you step 1 must be reduction. $\text{NO}_2$ is reduced to $\text{NH}_2$, with positions unchanged. So Q is the ortho amino acid, $\text{HOOCC}_6\text{H}_4\text{NH}_2$ with 1,2 relationship.

Decode R from step 2**
A primary aromatic amine with nitrous acid gives a diazonium salt. So the $\text{NH}_2$ in Q becomes $\text{N}_2^+$. R is therefore the same ortho substituted ring but with $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{N}^+\equiv\text{N}$ ortho to each other. This is the diazonium electrophile for the next step.

Decode S from the azo product**
Methyl red has structure $\text{HOOCC}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N(CH}_3)_2$ with the right hand $\text{N(CH}_3)_2$ para to the $\text{N=N}$ link. In azo coupling the $\text{N=N}$ comes from the diazonium R, and the rest of the right ring comes from S. S reacts like phenol, meaning it is a strongly activated ring. So S is simply $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N(CH}_3)_2$, $\text{N,N}$-dimethylaniline. Coupling occurs para to the $\text{N(CH}_3)_2$ group to give methyl red.

Final answer: Q: 2-aminobenzoic acid, benzene ring with $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{NH}_2$ ortho to each other (1,2-positions).
R: 2-carboxybenzenediazonium, benzene ring with $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{N}_2^+$ ($\text{N}^+\equiv\text{N}$) ortho to each other (1,2-positions).
S: $\text{N,N}$-dimethylaniline, benzene ring with $\text{N(CH}_3)_2$ group.

hints: Identify the type of change in step 1, $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$ is reduction, recall which metal in concentrated acid is used for nitroarenes.
Identify the type of change in step 2, $\text{NH}_2$ to diazonium requires in situ nitrous acid, think how $\text{HNO}_2$ is made.
Think about the very different temperature needs, one step needs vigorous heating and the other needs ice cold conditions to prevent decomposition.
walkthrough:
Choose reduction conditions for step 1**
Converting $\text{Ar-NO}_2$ to $\text{Ar-NH}_2$ needs six electrons, supplied by $\text{Fe}$ or $\text{Sn}$ in concentrated $\text{HCl}$. This reduction is slow, so you heat or reflux the mixture. The $\text{COOH}$ group survives these conditions.

Choose diazotisation reagents for step 2**
Converting $\text{Ar-NH}_2$ to $\text{Ar-N}_2^+$ uses nitrous acid, $\text{HNO}_2$, which is unstable so you make it fresh in the beaker from sodium nitrite, $\text{NaNO}_2$, plus $\text{HCl}$ (or $\text{NaNO}_2$ and $\text{HNO}_3$). The equation is $\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{HNO}_2 + \text{NaCl}$.

Control temperature carefully**
Diazonium salts decompose to phenols and nitrogen gas if warmed. So step 2 must be kept ice cold, below $10\,^\circ\text{C}$, typically 0 to $5\,^\circ\text{C}$. In contrast step 1 needs heat. Getting hot for reduction and cold for diazotisation is a classic exam distinction.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{Sn}$ / $\text{Fe}$ with conc. $\text{HCl}$, heat / reflux / hot.
step 2: $\text{NaNO}_2$ + $\text{HCl}$ (i.e. $\text{HNO}_2$) with temperature $\leqslant 10\,^\circ\text{C}$ (0 to 5 $^\circ\text{C}$).
